title: Sitting posture
hookLine: cross-legged, on a chair or a bench: a straight back, a relaxed body

cards: Take a quick inventory, right where you are. Is the head drifting forward toward a screen? Is one shoulder higher than the other?
Is the lower back curled like a question mark into the couch? Nothing wrong with any of it. That's just how bodies settle when nobody is paying attention.
Zen pays attention. Before any teaching about the mind, it starts with the body, and a very plain question: how are you sitting? Today's word: zazen.

teach.b: Zazen is Japanese for seated meditation: za, sitting, and zen, the meditation school's own word. A plain name for the school's central practice. First, the base.

The classic postures are cross-legged on a firm round cushion: full lotus, each foot resting on the opposite thigh; half lotus, one foot up; or the easier Burmese way, both legs folded on the floor, one in front of the other.

teach.h: A STABLE BASE: CUSHION, BENCH, CHAIR.
teach.b: Some people kneel, on a cushion or a small wooden bench. Some sit on a chair, feet flat, not leaning back. Zen teachers today offer these.
The point isn't the shape of the legs. It's a base stable enough that the body can stop holding itself up by effort. Then the spine.
It rises straight, not stiff, more stacked than braced. Some teachers describe a thread lifting gently from the crown of the head.

teach.h: EARS OVER SHOULDERS, NOSE OVER NAVEL.
teach.b: There's an old instruction, which this path will read in full later, from Dogen's guide to sitting: ears in line with the shoulders, nose in line with the navel. Anyone can check it.
Then the pair: straight and relaxed. Straight alone turns into a soldier at attention, tight in the jaw and shoulders, and soon tired. Relaxed alone slumps back into the couch.
Zazen asks for both at once: upright enough to stay awake, soft enough to stay there.

how: In Zen centers and monasteries, people sit zazen facing a wall or the room, on round cushions over flat mats, on kneeling benches or on chairs, and beginners are usually shown how to find their posture before anything else.

games.q: you want to try zazen, but your knees won't let you cross your legs. what do you do?
o: skip zazen; it isn't for you
sit on a chair or a bench, back upright
games.why: a chair or a kneeling bench is a real zazen posture. the point is a stable base, a straight back and a relaxed body.

practice: Come to the front of whatever you're sitting on, let the base settle, and rock gently side to side and forward and back, each sway smaller, until you stop in the middle.
Ears over shoulders, nose over navel; then let the shoulders drop and the belly soften. Straight and relaxed, simply sit there in that shape.

wordCard.voice: Zazen. Japanese for seated meditation, the central practice of Zen: a stable base, a straight back, a relaxed body. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: za, sitting, and zen, meditation; seated meditation.

carryVoice: Your line: straight and relaxed. A cushion, a bench or a chair all count. Back tomorrow with the hands.
